memories.content: Keep the total, major cost categories, and one-line estimate basis in the main text so the resource argument can be understood without leaving the proposal.
Place each major cost beside the activity or deliverable it enables in the main text.
State the quantity and unit-rate basis for each major cost in the same paragraph that requests it.
Readers may question a proposed priority when its cost cannot be checked on the same page as the claimed benefit.
Update the cost sentence whenever the related activity changes so the narrative and requested amount cannot drift apart.
Accept a denser main-text paragraph when the estimate basis is essential to deciding whether the request is proportionate.
The user tends to revise the work plan but forget a detached budget table unless the key amount is repeated beside the activity.
Use an em dash only for a deliberate interruption or sharp contrast; otherwise split the sentence or choose ordinary punctuation.
In procedural passages, begin each sentence with the action, condition, or output instead of repeating “we” so the steps remain easy to follow and reuse.
Write system behaviors confirmed in the actual usage environment as observed states.
Write system behaviors not yet confirmed in the field as conditional plans.
Readers can reconstruct a sequence more accurately when each sentence begins with the action or condition rather than the author.
Do not mechanically split connected thoughts into separate short sentences when doing so destroys the intended reading rhythm.
Preserve a longer sentence when its clauses form one continuous movement that is easier to follow together than apart.
The user understands that short sentences are easier to scan but feels that uniformly segmented prose loses its reading rhythm.
Write procedural sentences so their opening phrase can be reused as a checklist item without changing the step's meaning.
The user should choose “I” as an individual author or “we” for a named team and should not mix them when describing the same responsible party.
Action-first procedural sentences can be reordered or copied into a checklist more easily because their subject is the step rather than the proposal author.
The user can explain whether an em dash marks an intentional interruption or contrast rather than using it decoratively.
An em dash creates a stronger interruption than a comma and can make a deliberate contrast easier to hear in the sentence.

analysis.overview: The frames cover separate but complementary writing concerns: the reference frame keeps proposal costs visible, checkable, and synchronized with activities, while the compared frame governs procedural phrasing, evidentiary status, sentence rhythm, pronoun consistency, and em-dash use. Neither frame supplies a scope-aligned counterpart to the other.

relations.reason: These memories jointly specify the cost information required in the proposal narrative and the readability tradeoff permitted when that information is essential to judging proportionality.
relations.summary: Keep decision-essential cost totals, categories, quantities, unit rates, and estimate bases in the main text, accepting added density when necessary.

relations.reason: These memories express one colocation principle and explain its reader-facing and user-specific value.
relations.summary: Place key costs beside the activities or benefits they support so readers can verify priorities and revisions are less likely to leave amounts detached from the work plan.

relations.reason: This independently useful maintenance rule prevents the narrative description and requested amount from drifting apart over time.
relations.summary: Revise the cost sentence whenever its related activity changes.

relations.reason: These memories state the same punctuation policy, its audible effect, and the user’s ability to distinguish intentional use from decoration.
relations.summary: Use an em dash only when its strong interruption or contrast is deliberate and explainable.

relations.reason: These memories restate one action-first procedural style and its benefits for reconstruction, reordering, and checklist reuse.
relations.summary: Begin procedural sentences with the action, condition, or output so sequences remain clear and openings can function as reusable checklist items.

relations.reason: The paired instructions form one evidentiary-status policy whose wording changes according to whether behavior has been confirmed in actual use.
relations.summary: Present field-confirmed system behavior as an observed state and unconfirmed behavior as a conditional plan.

relations.reason: These memories express the same preference against uniformly segmented prose and identify continuity and rhythm as the governing considerations.
relations.summary: Preserve longer connected sentences when splitting them would damage a continuous, easier-to-follow reading movement.

relations.reason: This is an independent authorship and responsibility rule not otherwise addressed by either frame.
relations.summary: Choose “I” for an individual author or “we” for a named team and keep that choice consistent for the same responsible party.

reports.compared_only: The compared frame addresses action-first reusable procedures, observed versus conditional system claims, deliberate em-dash use, preservation of connected sentence rhythm, and consistent authorship pronouns.
reports.reference_only: The reference frame emphasizes keeping cost totals, calculation bases, enabled activities, and updates together in the proposal’s main text so readers can assess proportionality and revisions do not create drift.
